lesson.title: Logic: switches that decide
lesson.subtitle: AND, OR and NOT, and the rules every smart device runs

video.title: Logic: switches that decide
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Amina in an empty, sunny classroom; a ceiling fan spins over empty desks. A coin drops into a meter.
scenes.animation: The fan spins; coins fall one by one.
scenes.narration: Our classroom fan runs all afternoon, even when the room is empty. That wastes power and money. I want it on only when it's hot and someone is in the room. That isn't a gadget problem. It's a logic problem.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: logic, the switches that make decisions inside every device.

scenes.visual: A switch flips; a big 1 appears, then a 0. A box labelled 'gate' takes two wires in and sends one out.
scenes.animation: 1 and 0 flip in turn; the gate box draws its wires.
scenes.narration: Inside a device, every signal is either on or off. We write on as one and off as zero, or say true and false. A logic gate takes one or two of these inputs, and gives one output. Three gates do most of the work: AND, OR and NOT.

scenes.visual: Two switches in a row on one wire to a lamp. Close one: dark. Close both: light.
scenes.animation: Switch A closes, nothing; switch B closes, the lamp lights.
scenes.narration: AND is on only when both inputs are on. Wire two switches one after the other, in series, and the lamp lights only when both are closed. Hot AND someone in the room: that's our fan.

scenes.visual: Two switches side by side, each on its own path to the lamp. Either one lights it.
scenes.animation: Switch A closes: light. Open it, close B: light.
scenes.narration: OR is on when either input is on, or both. Wire two switches side by side, in parallel, and closing either one lights the lamp. Two doors, one alarm: front door open OR back door open.

scenes.visual: A fridge door closes on a small button: the inside light goes out. It opens: the button springs out and the light comes on.
scenes.animation: Door swings shut and open; the button springs.
scenes.narration: NOT flips its input: on becomes off, and off becomes on. A fridge light is a NOT. When the door is shut, it presses the switch and the light is off. Open the door, the switch is no longer pressed, and the light comes on.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor by the school gate with two buttons on a post; only one is lit. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our school gate opens only if the guard presses his button AND a teacher presses hers. This morning, only the guard presses. Does the gate open?

scenes.visual: The gate stays closed; one lit button, one dark, and a cross badge. A second hand presses; the gate swings open.
scenes.animation: Cross badge pops; then the second press and the gate opens.
scenes.narration: It stays shut. AND needs both inputs on, so one button isn't enough. That's the whole point: two people must agree.

scenes.visual: A four-row table builds on a chalkboard: A, B, AND, OR.
scenes.animation: Rows write in one by one; the AND column fills, then the OR column.
scenes.narration: A truth table lists every combination of inputs, with the output for each. Two inputs give four rows. For AND, only the last row is on. For OR, only the first row is off.

scenes.visual: A staircase with a switch at each end; a lamp halfway. Then the same rule appears as a line of code on a small board.
scenes.animation: Bottom switch flips: on. Top switch flips: off. Code types in.
scenes.narration: Real rules combine gates. A stair light has a switch at the bottom and one at the top, and either one changes it. It's on when the two switches differ, a gate called XOR. A microcontroller runs exactly these rules, written in code.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma beside a rooftop water tank and a pump with heat lines. Thumbs-up and thumbs-down cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our water tank alarm beeps if the tank is nearly empty OR the pump is overheating. The tank is full, but the pump is overheating. Does it beep?

scenes.visual: Three gate symbols line up, then a small truth table.
scenes.animation: Symbols line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Yes, it beeps: OR needs only one input on. Remember: AND needs all its inputs, OR needs any one, and NOT flips. A truth table checks every case.

scenes.visual: Pupils at the front with 1 and 0 cards; a truth table for the fan on the board.
scenes.animation: Cards flip; the table fills in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: human logic gates. Give pairs of pupils cards with one and zero, and let a third pupil be the gate. Then write the fan rule as a truth table on the board. Next time: how a device stores numbers in bits.

checkpoints.prompt: The gate opens only if the guard AND a teacher press their buttons. Only the guard presses. Does it open?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — AND needs both inputs on. One button gives 1 AND 0, which is 0.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — AND needs both inputs on, so one button isn't enough: 1 AND 0 is 0.

checkpoints.prompt: The alarm beeps if the tank is nearly empty OR the pump overheats. The tank is full; the pump overheats. Does it beep?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — OR needs only one input on: 0 OR 1 is 1.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with OR, one input on is enough. The overheating pump alone sets it off.
